messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Restrained): Feeling physically restrained or held down, Conflict: Confrontations, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh was seventy-six years old and still working the night shift at a regional distribution warehouse, stacking boxes of canned goods onto pallets. He had been a civilian in Phnom Penh during the years of forced evacuation and labor camps, and what he remembered most clearly was the smell of smoke and wet earth, and the feeling of rope around his wrists. He had been taken from his village by soldiers when he was eighteen, tied with other young men to a wooden beam in a barn, and held there for three days without food. The rope was coarse and tight, and every time he tried to shift his weight it bit deeper into his skin. He could still feel it, sometimes, when he woke in the dark.

The memory came without warning. One minute he would be sliding a box onto a shelf, the next he would be back in that barn, the smell of diesel exhaust from a forklift suddenly becoming the smell of the soldiers’ truck, his chest tightening so fast that he had to put down the box and lean against a stack of pallets. The vividness of it—the exact grain of the wood, the angle of the light through a crack in the wall—terrified him more than the memory itself, because it meant he had lost control. He would stand there, shaking, his breath shallow, until a coworker called his name or a supervisor clapped him on the shoulder, and then he would flinch away from the touch. Being held down by a sudden grip, even a friendly one, made his stomach drop.

Confrontations were worse. In the warehouse, disputes over shift schedules or misplaced inventory were common, and Minh had learned to keep his head down. But one afternoon a younger worker accused him of leaving a pallet in the wrong aisle, raising his voice, stepping closer. Minh’s hands went numb. He could not speak. He backed away, turned, and walked out the back door, leaving his jacket and his lunch behind. He stood in the alley for twenty minutes, staring at a brick wall, repeating to himself that he was not tied up, that he could leave anytime. The man had not touched him, but the raised voice and the looming posture had been enough. After that, Minh started taking his breaks alone in the bathroom, eating a banana over the sink so no one would approach him.

The smells were the hardest. The warehouse stored cleaning supplies, and the scent of bleach sometimes drifted across the loading dock. It reminded him of the chemical smell in the camp latrines, which mingled with the smoke from burning garbage. His nose would fill with it, and suddenly the memory was not just a picture but a full-body experience—the ache in his shoulders from being bound, the dry grit in his mouth, the terror of not knowing when it would end. He had learned to breathe through his mouth when he entered certain aisles, and he avoided the cleaning supply section entirely, even if it meant taking a longer route to the break room. His supervisor had noticed, and twice had asked him why he was walking around the long way. Minh had shrugged and said his knees hurt.

The consequences of these habits had grown quietly over the years. He lived alone in a small apartment with a kitchen table he never sat at, because the chair had a straight back that reminded him of leaning against the wooden beam. He ate standing at the counter. He had no contact with his surviving relatives—he had stopped answering the phone years ago, because hearing a voice he did not expect, even a familiar one, felt like an ambush. He had never married. The warehouse was the only place he went outside of his apartment, and even there he had become invisible, arriving early, leaving late, speaking to no one unless forced.

What brought him to the clinic was a panic attack so severe that a coworker called an ambulance. Minh had been walking past a pallet of bottled water when a loose plastic strap caught his ankle. The sudden resistance, the sensation of being held in place, had thrown him into the past so completely that he fell to his knees, sobbing. The EMTs found him curled against a stack of boxes, repeating a Khmer word they did not understand. He was taken to the emergency room, cleared medically, and referred to a specialty clinic for trauma. When the intake worker asked him what he hoped for, Minh sat in silence for a long time. Then he said, very quietly, that he wanted to be able to walk past a pallet of water without falling apart. He did not say that he was also afraid of what would happen if he ever had to feel the rope again—because that, he was certain, would break him entirely.
